questions.prompt: In Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey, a person aged 15 or over without a job is classified as unemployed only if the person
options: is receiving Employment Insurance benefits
has looked for work in the last 4 weeks
has been without a job for at least 4 weeks
has no source of income
questions.explanation: The key criterion on the slide is that the person **has looked for work in the last 4 weeks** (and is without a job). Someone without a job who has not searched is classified as *not in the labour force*, whether or not they receive EI.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would cause the measured unemployment rate to overstate true joblessness?
options: Discouraged workers stop looking for work
Part-time workers who want full-time jobs are counted as fully employed
Some people report looking for work only to remain eligible for EI
Workers increase their search effort after a recession
questions.explanation: Overstating: people who claim to look for work to stay eligible for EI are counted as unemployed even though they are not really searching (and some workers hide informal or illegal employment). The first two options *understate* joblessness: discouraged workers drop out of the labour force, and underemployed part-timers are counted as fully employed.

questions.prompt: In a country the working-age population is 30,000, of whom 18,000 are employed and 2,000 are unemployed (the rest are not in the labour force). What is the unemployment rate, in percent?
questions.explanation: Labour force = 18,000 + 2,000 = 20,000. Unemployment rate = 2,000 ÷ 20,000 × 100 = **10%**. (The participation rate is 20,000 ÷ 30,000 × 100 ≈ 66.7%.) Dividing by the working-age population instead of the labour force is the classic mistake.

questions.prompt: A manufacturing plant closes because demand for its cars collapses in a recession, and its workers are laid off. This is mainly which type of unemployment?
options: Frictional
Structural
Seasonal
Cyclical
questions.explanation: **Cyclical unemployment** is caused by a business-cycle recession: demand for goods and services falls, firms cut production and lay off workers (the slide's example is the 2009 Chrysler plant closure in Brampton). Frictional = matching/search; structural = persistent skills mismatch; seasonal = predictable changes in labour demand through the year.

questions.prompt: According to the slides, the natural rate of unemployment (the full-employment rate) equals
options: frictional plus structural unemployment
frictional plus cyclical unemployment
structural plus cyclical unemployment
the sum of all four types of unemployment
questions.explanation: The natural rate = **frictional + structural** unemployment; it is the rate when cyclical unemployment is zero (full employment). It is a theoretical concept that must be estimated, since it cannot be measured directly. Seasonal unemployment is handled through seasonal adjustment, not through the natural rate.

questions.prompt: A 45-year-old worker whose skills no longer match the jobs available in her region needs retraining before she can get a job. Compared with frictional unemployment, her unemployment is
options: shorter and always avoidable
associated with longer unemployment spells
caused by a fall in aggregate demand
predictable and tied to the time of year
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment comes from a persistent mismatch between workers' skills and the jobs available, and is **associated with longer unemployment spells**. Frictional unemployment is short-term job-search unemployment (and can even improve job matches).

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not one of the three key factors the slides use to explain frictional and structural unemployment?
options: Government policies
Labour unions
Efficiency wages
The CPI basket
questions.explanation: The three factors are **government policies** (e.g. EI, minimum wage laws), **labour unions** and **efficiency wages**. The CPI basket is part of measuring inflation, not explaining unemployment.

questions.prompt: How does Employment Insurance (EI) tend to affect unemployment, according to the slides?
options: It raises the opportunity cost of searching, so spells shorten
It lowers the opportunity cost of job search, so workers may search longer before accepting a job
It has no effect because benefits are taxed
It raises cyclical unemployment only
questions.explanation: EI replaces part of lost earnings (55% up to a weekly maximum), which **lowers the opportunity cost of job search**. Workers search longer for a better match, which can lengthen unemployment but may improve match quality and productivity.

questions.prompt: An efficiency wage is
options: the minimum wage set by a province
a wage negotiated by a labour union
an above-market wage a firm pays to raise workers' productivity
the wage at which the labour market clears
questions.explanation: An efficiency wage is an **above-market wage paid to increase productivity** (workers work hard to keep a well-paid job when monitoring is costly). Because it keeps wages above equilibrium it is another reason unemployment exists even when cyclical unemployment is zero.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the GDP deflator and the CPI is correct?
options: The CPI is available quarterly; the GDP deflator is available monthly
The GDP deflator includes imports and excludes exports
The GDP deflator is available quarterly, includes exports and excludes imports, so it is not ideal for measuring households' cost of living
The CPI measures the prices of all final goods produced domestically
questions.explanation: The GDP deflator (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100) covers all final goods and services produced domestically: it is **quarterly, includes exports and excludes imports**. The CPI is **monthly** and better reflects household living costs because it covers the basket households buy (including imports).

questions.prompt: The CPI is 161 in 2024 and 164 in 2025. What is the CPI-based inflation rate between 2024 and 2025, in percent (to two decimals)?

Base year 2025: the basket (400 ginger ales, 200 samosas, 12 bus passes) costs $3,120 at base-year prices ($1.50, $6.00, $110). The next year prices are $1.60, $8.00 and $130, so the same basket costs $3,800. What is the CPI in the next year (one decimal)?
questions.explanation: CPI = cost of the basket at current prices ÷ cost at base-year prices × 100 = 3,800 ÷ 3,120 × 100 ≈ **121.8**. (By construction the CPI is 100 in the base year.)

questions.prompt: Households switch from boutiques to warehouse stores when prices rise, but the CPI's constant basket ignores this. This is called
options: substitution bias
outlet bias
new product bias
increase in quality bias
questions.explanation: **Outlet bias**: consumers change *where* they shop. Substitution bias is switching to *different goods* when a price rises; new product bias is new goods missing from the basket; quality bias is price rises that partly reflect better quality. All four make the CPI **overstate** inflation.

questions.prompt: According to the slides, the four CPI biases cause measured CPI inflation to
options: understate true inflation by 0.5 to 1 percentage point
overstate true inflation by 0.5 to 1 percentage point
overstate true inflation by 5 to 10 percentage points
have no net effect on measured inflation
questions.explanation: The biases (quality, substitution, new product, outlet) make changes in the CPI **overstate the true rate of inflation by 0.5 to 1 percentage point**. Note the direction: overstate, not understate.

questions.prompt: The Producer Price Index (PPI) is useful because it
options: measures the prices of imports only
can give early warning of future movements in consumer prices
is based on the same basket as the CPI
replaces the GDP deflator in the national accounts
questions.explanation: The PPI averages prices received by producers at all stages of production, including intermediate goods and raw materials. If those prices rise, costs of final goods rise, so it **gives early warning of future consumer-price movements**. Its basket is of producer goods, not the household basket.

questions.prompt: Your mother earned $30,000 in April 1996 (CPI = 89). The CPI in April 2026 is 168. How many 2026 dollars have the same purchasing power as $30,000 in 1996? (nearest dollar)
questions.explanation: Value in 2026 dollars = 30,000 × 168 ÷ 89 ≈ **$56,629**. Your $60,000 job is therefore only about 6% richer in real terms (60,000 ÷ 56,629), not twice as rich, because the price level rose by a factor of 168/89 ≈ 1.9.

questions.prompt: City A pays $60,000 a year and City B pays $63,000. Monthly rent is $1,500 in A and $2,000 in B; other monthly costs are $3,500 in both cities. By what percent is the total cost of living higher in City B than in City A?
questions.explanation: Monthly cost: A = 1,500 + 3,500 = $5,000; B = 2,000 + 3,500 = $5,500. Difference = 500 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = **10%**. Income is only 5% higher in B ((63,000 − 60,000) ÷ 60,000), and rent alone is 33% higher.

questions.prompt: In the two-city job offer (A: $60,000, B: $63,000, other costs $3,500 a month in both, rent $1,500 in A and $2,000 in B), what is the best decision?
options: Take B: income is 5% higher
Take B: rent is only 33% higher while income is higher
Take A: living costs are 10% higher in B but income only 5% higher
Indifferent: the two differences cancel
questions.explanation: Cost of living is 10% higher in B but income only 5% higher, so purchasing power is lower in B (annual income minus costs: A $60,000 - $60,000 = $0 vs B $63,000 - $66,000 = -$3,000). **Take A.** Comparing nominal income alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: You save $1,000 at 4% for a year. A pizza+drink combo costs $10 now and $10.30 next year. After one year, the % change in the number of combos you can buy (your real return) is closest to what percent? (two decimals)
questions.explanation: Now: $1,000 ÷ $10 = 100 combos. A year later: $1,040 ÷ $10.30 ≈ 100.97 combos, a rise of **about 0.97%**. The shortcut r = i − π = 4% − 3% = 1% is a close approximation.

questions.prompt: A loan carries a nominal rate of 7%. Borrower and lender anticipated 4% inflation (an anticipated real rate of 3%), but inflation turns out to be 2%. What is the actual real interest rate, in percent?
questions.explanation: Real rate ≈ nominal − actual inflation = 7% − 2% = **5%**. Inflation was lower than expected, so the lender gains (real return 5% instead of 3%) and the borrower loses.

questions.prompt: You buy a one-year GIC with a guaranteed rate of 3.5%. You anticipated 1.5% inflation (a 2% real return), but inflation turns out to be 3.5%. What is your actual real return, in percent?
questions.explanation: Real return ≈ 3.5% − 3.5% = **0%**. Unanticipated inflation made saving risky: the guaranteed nominal return did not protect purchasing power.

questions.prompt: If the economy is experiencing deflation,
options: the nominal interest rate will be equal to the real interest rate.
the nominal interest rate will be lower than the real interest rate.
the nominal interest rate will be higher than the real interest rate.
high nominal interest rates inflict serious losses on both household and business borrowers.
questions.explanation: Real rate = nominal - inflation. Under deflation, inflation is negative, so subtracting it **adds** to the nominal rate: the real rate is *higher* than the nominal rate, i.e. the nominal rate is lower than the real rate.

questions.prompt: Since nominal incomes increase with inflation,
options: expected inflation does not affect the purchasing power of the average consumer.
expected inflation reduces the purchasing power of the average consumer.
expected inflation increases the purchasing power of the average consumer.
unexpected inflation does not affect the purchasing power of the average consumer.
questions.explanation: If nominal incomes rise along with prices, and inflation is expected so people adjust, the purchasing power of the **average** consumer is not changed by expected inflation. Unexpected inflation, by contrast, redistributes income and wealth and creates risk. (The slides stress that even anticipated inflation has costs through uneven adjustment, menu costs and cash holdings; this item is about the average consumer's purchasing power.)

questions.prompt: Suppose the inflation rate turns out to be much higher than most people expected. In that case,
options: a borrower will gain from the situation while a lender will lose.
a lender will gain from the situation while a borrower will lose.
both borrower and lender will gain from the situation.
both borrower and lender will lose in this situation.
questions.explanation: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the real interest rate (nominal rate fixed in the contract, inflation higher). The **borrower repays in dollars worth less**, so the borrower gains and the lender loses.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the costs of inflation is correct?
options: Only unanticipated inflation imposes any costs
Anticipated inflation causes menu costs and taxes on nominal returns, while unanticipated inflation makes lending riskier so banks become more cautious about lending
Anticipated inflation raises the real value of cash holdings
Unanticipated inflation is harmless if all wages are indexed to the CPI
questions.explanation: Even **anticipated** inflation has costs: unequal income adjustment, diminished real value of cash, menu costs, and taxes on nominal (not real) returns. **Unanticipated** inflation adds risk to borrowing and lending, with the result that **banks become more cautious about lending**.
